heading: THE BIG WINNERS AND LOSERS IN US WEBSITE TRAFFIC OVER THE PAST YEAR (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: Using Semrush Traffic Analytics data comparing July 2026 to July 2025, the article reveals significant shifts in U.S. website traffic despite apparent stability at the top. Google and YouTube remain dominant but grew 10.72% and 36.6% respectively, with the top three sites now generating 54.3% of the top 10's traffic. ChatGPT emerged as the clearest winner, ranking ninth with 1.09 billion monthly visits and a 48.38% year-over-year increase, surpassing DuckDuckGo and Bing. Major losers include Bing (down 50.43%), Amazon (down 15.31%), and DuckDuckGo (down 15.83%), though their declines stem from different causes ranging from failed AI integration to policy changes and platform shifts. The article warns that GA4's attribution capabilities are deteriorating as AI chat interfaces strip referrer data, leaving SEOs blind to traffic sources—with one tracked publisher seeing direct traffic climb from 62.5% to 78% of total sessions, mostly unattributable visits likely from ChatGPT and similar tools.
strategic_hook: Organizations need to understand which customer acquisition channels are actually driving traffic and conversions by supplementing deteriorating GA4 data with audience intelligence platforms (Semrush, SparkToro, GWI) and direct customer research (surveys, panels) to map where target customers discover and engage with their content.

heading: STREAMING IS RAISING PRICES FASTER THAN CABLE EVER DID (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Streaming services have raised prices three times faster than inflation since 2022, with major platforms delivering dramatic increases: Apple TV has tripled from $4.99 to nearly $15, Disney+ jumped 172 percent from its $6.99 launch price to $11.99 with ads, and Netflix Premium is up 125 percent since 2013. A full lineup of eight major ad-free streamers now costs approximately $151 monthly compared to $90 four years ago, while over the past year streaming rates collectively rose 11.8 percent—far outpacing the 3.84 percent annual consumer inflation rate. The article notes that cable and satellite TV historically averaged only 3.9 percent annual price increases, making streaming's trajectory substantially steeper than the cord-cutting alternative that consumers originally fled. Gen Z has reportedly responded by "streaming cycling"—rotating monthly subscriptions to avoid paying for multiple services simultaneously—but this approach means missing watercooler moments and falling behind on shows.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: THE BEST ADS DON'T CREATE DESIRE, THEY BORROW IT (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article argues that effective advertising doesn't create desire but rather taps into existing human wants and aims them at a product. Drawing on Eugene Schwartz's work and Drew Eric Whitman's Life-Force 8 framework—eight biologically programmed wants including survival, sexual companionship, freedom from fear, social approval, and superiority—the piece demonstrates how legendary ads across three centuries (1923 Listerine's "Often a bridesmaid," 1940s Charles Atlas, 1926 U.S. School of Music, and Dove's 2004 Campaign for Real Beauty) succeeded by identifying which deep desire their audience already possessed and then staging vivid scenes that made readers feel the benefit rather than merely stating it. The copywriting technique involves naming the specific obstacle standing between customers and their desired outcome (Listerine's "halitosis," for example) and positioning the product as its removal. The article concludes that the real power in persuasion comes from the market's existing desires, not from the advertiser's creativity.
strategic_hook: Understanding which of the eight Life-Force desires your product actually serves allows you to identify and address the genuine customer needs that drive purchase decisions, moving beyond feature-based messaging to emotional resonance.

heading: SHE PAID PEOPLE TO CANCEL HER COMPETITOR (2 MINUTE READ)

Beyond the acquisition angle, the strategy built direct messaging relationships with switchers and created built-in opportunities to collect competitive intelligence about why customers left rivals and what they were previously paying.
strategic_hook: This tactic provides direct customer research into competitor strengths and pricing by capturing reasons for switching and competitor pricing data through the cancellation-screenshot requirement, enabling competitive positioning and pricing strategy refinement.

The confusion around Disavow stems from 2012-era algorithmic penalties via Google's Penguin update, but since 2016 when Penguin became part of the core algorithm, low-quality links only devalue individual pages rather than triggering sitewide penalties. Without a manual penalty, there is nothing to recover from, making Disavow unnecessary for most sites today. Instead, recovery strategies should focus on quality content, superior user experience, and outreach to trustworthy sites for legitimate links.

heading: HOW NETFLIX MEASURES THE MARKETING YOU CANNOT A/B TEST (5 MINUTE READ)
summary: Netflix and other sophisticated marketing organizations use geo experiments—randomizing geographic markets rather than individual users—to measure the causal impact of marketing channels that cannot be A/B tested at the individual level, such as billboards, television, and sponsorships. Google published the foundational methodology in 2011, and Netflix has industrialized the approach through an internal tool called Quasimodo, which handles the constraint of small sample sizes by treating each campaign removal and relaunch as additional independent measurements of the same effect. The critical success factors are not statistical but organizational: leadership must make binding decisions about holdout size (trading measurement confidence against media delivery), protect test windows from contamination by national campaigns, honestly bound the duration of effects being measured, and repeat tests on a rolling cadence to accumulate stable understanding rather than one-off anecdotes. The author proposes a standard requiring every channel receiving 8 figures annually to have a market-level causal read less than 24 months old with pre-registered analysis and adequate power, yet most organizations fail this standard not from lack of methodology but from lack of executive commitment to demand it.
strategic_hook: Understanding which marketing channels drive genuine incremental sales requires designing measurement programs that match channel mechanics, helping leadership allocate budgets based on validated causal evidence rather than attributed reporting or narrative justification.

strategic_hook: Marketing leaders need to evaluate whether AI automation projects genuinely reduce execution time on core customer-acquisition activities versus simply shifting hours from revenue-generating work to tool-building and maintenance, requiring transparent tracking of time allocation to inform resource prioritization decisions.

heading: THE 11X ROAS ACCOUNT THAT LOST MONEY ON EVERY ORDER (5 MINUTE READ)
summary: An ecommerce account reporting an impressive 11x ROAS was actually losing money on every order due to hidden costs excluded from the ROAS calculation. The article reveals a real case study where a £100 apparel order with reported conversion value of £100 yielded only £60 net revenue after VAT, lost £28 to a 28% return rate, and after subtracting COGS (63%), fulfillment, shipping, and payment fees, resulted in a negative £0.39 contribution per order. The 11x figure was also blended, mixing brand campaigns at 18x ROAS (which would largely have converted organically) with nonbrand at 3x, inflating the headline number while masking poor true incremental performance. Additionally, tuning campaigns for maximum efficiency created a second hidden loss by reducing volume so severely that seasonal inventory aged into deep markdowns below cost rather than converting to cash during the selling window. The author recommends rebuilding conversion values as contribution margins, separating brand and nonbrand performance, assigning each SKU a single commercial objective, and making cash-flow decisions transparently rather than optimizing toward platform-reported metrics.
strategic_hook: Understanding the full customer acquisition economics—including returns, fulfillment costs, and working capital impacts—is essential to building accurate business cases and determining whether paid media investments genuinely improve profitability versus merely inflating misleading top-line metrics.

heading: THE AFTERMARKET PREMIUM (6 MINUTE READ)
summary: The aftermarket—businesses that modify and enhance existing platforms—is a repeatable company archetype that has produced major businesses like AMG, Singer, Red Hat, and Cursor. Platform owners face four strategic responses to aftermarket modifiers: coexist (as Porsche does with Singer restomods), fight (as Rolex initially did with watch customizers), license (as LVMH did with Bamford), or acquire (as Mercedes did with AMG in 2005). In physical goods, aftermarket layers form slowly over decades due to capital intensity, but in software they emerge rapidly when platforms are open-source or ship modding tools—Microsoft's VS Code spawned Cursor, which SpaceX acquired for $60 billion in June 2026, while closed platforms prevent aftermarkets entirely through legal barriers. The article identifies espresso machines and robotics (via the Robot Operating System) as emerging categories where aftermarket layers may soon form, predicting that as AI reduces development costs, aftermarket businesses will proliferate wherever open platforms exist.
strategic_hook: Understanding which markets have the preconditions for profitable aftermarket ecosystems—obsessive user communities, durable platforms, capital-intensive modifications, and (for software) open architecture—helps identify where to build modifier businesses or how platform owners should position their openness strategy.

heading: SEEING LIKE A STATE (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: In this essay adapted from James C. Scott's "Seeing Like a State," author Mike Fisher uses the cautionary tale of eighteenth-century Prussian scientific forestry to explore how organizations risk destroying what makes them work by over-optimizing for legible metrics. When Prussia's foresters simplified complex old-growth forests into monoculture rows to maximize timber yield, yields initially soared but eventually collapsed by 20-30 percent as the invisible soil ecosystem was consumed; the system succeeded only by burning accumulated capital it could not measure. Fisher applies this "legibility" concept to modern corporate life, showing how dashboards, KPIs, org charts, and systems like Microsoft's stack-ranking render organizations readable but destroy the illegible "metis"—the practical, experiential knowledge of individual contributors—that actually makes enterprises function. Stack ranking at Microsoft exemplified this perfectly: it accurately measured performance on a bell curve while systematically eroding the collaboration and trust that drive software engineering, until Lisa Brummel abolished it in 2013. The essay concludes that leaders must hold their simplifications with humility, deliberately audit metrics against ground truth, and protect pockets of productive illegibility rather than standardizing everything visible.
strategic_hook: When designing customer research and journey-mapping initiatives, identify which customer behaviors and organizational capabilities your measurement system is blind to, so you avoid optimizing toward metrics that destroy the relationship quality or informal coordination mechanisms that actually drive customer satisfaction and retention.

Two key tactical approaches are highlighted: repurposing blog content as LinkedIn articles (800–1,200 words) to improve AI search visibility and ranking, and using LinkedIn Thought Leader ads to amplify organic posts that perform well. The strategy requires treating LinkedIn as a numbers game—posting frequently and testing messaging with real audiences—and securing executive buy-in by starting small, proving results through attribution, and using tools like Fibbler or Clay to track influence on deals and pipeline.
strategic_hook: This directly supports customer strategy by identifying the messaging, tone, and content angles that resonate most with target buyers, which informs both positioning refinement and the narrative foundation for customer acquisition campaigns.

heading: WHY AI HASN'T SOLVED MARKETING'S TIME PROBLEM (5 MINUTE READ)

The real bottlenecks are approvals and sign-offs (47% of delays), design and production (38%), and team coordination (36%), not copywriting. AI generates more options, which paradoxically increases decision-making burden and cognitive load rather than streamlining it; 88% of teams report their AI output still requires moderate to substantial human editing for brand alignment and strategy. Teams that successfully use AI complete campaigns faster by deploying the technology strategically at workflow bottlenecks and standardizing processes, suggesting the problem lies not with AI itself but with fragmented, approval-heavy production workflows that remain unexamined.
strategic_hook: Marketing teams need to map their end-to-end campaign production workflow and identify the true bottlenecks (approvals, handoffs, decision complexity) before selecting AI tools, because deploying AI without addressing systemic workflow problems wastes efficiency gains and creates more work rather than freeing capacity for strategy.

heading: IS THE LIKE BUTTON DEAD? (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Social media engagement metrics are fundamentally shifting away from likes and comments toward passive consumption signals like watch time and completion rates. Data from Anthropic's analysis of 2.5 million Instagram posts shows average likes on carousels dropped 73% and on Reels dropped 81% between January 2025 and May 2026, with top-tier content also experiencing 54%+ engagement declines. Platform algorithms now prioritize watch time, completion rates, replays, and dwell time rather than interaction metrics—TikTok tracks micro-watches, Instagram measures carousel dwell time, and LinkedIn weights reading duration as primary ranking signals. Rather than building community through comments, social media marketers need to focus on hooks to capture attention and optimize for watch-through rates as their core KPIs in this new era of interest-based algorithmic distribution.
strategic_hook: Customer strategy teams should reassess how they measure social media effectiveness for customer engagement and brand awareness campaigns, shifting from vanity metrics (likes/comments) to view-through and watch-time data that better reflect actual customer interest signals in algorithmic environments.

heading: ENTITIES ARE THE FOUNDATION OF MODERN SEO (10 MINUTE READ)
summary: Entity SEO—ensuring that search engines and AI systems accurately understand who your brand is—has become foundational to modern information retrieval, building on Google's 15-year history with the Knowledge Graph. The author argues that entity clarity requires three parallel efforts: owning and maintaining consistent brand information across controlled properties (websites, profiles, structured data), describing each page's target entity with credible supporting content, and earning third-party corroboration through quality mentions and citations. Key practices include auditing owned properties for consistency (name, address, phone, author credentials), building entity maps that show relationships between your organization and connected people, products, services and topics, and monitoring "entity drift" as your online presence grows. The approach extends beyond traditional backlink-focused SEO to emphasize reputation corroboration, with tools like Named Entity Recognition helping extract and classify entities at scale. In a landscape where Google removed three billion entities from its Knowledge Graph in 2025 to reduce ambiguity, clarity and consistency in how you represent yourself has become competitively critical.
strategic_hook: Understanding how search systems and LLMs perceive your brand's identity and positioning versus competitors directly informs market positioning strategy and reveals where customer perception may diverge from intended brand identity.

heading: PAID IS NOW THE ONLY GUARANTEED SLOT IN AN AI ANSWER (5 MINUTE READ)
summary: OpenAI's ChatGPT Ads have reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate roughly 200 days after launch, with the self-serve platform now available in forty-plus countries as of late August 2026. The key shift is that paid sponsored cards now appear directly within conversational AI answers alongside organic citations, creating a single frame where only the ad slot is purchasable—a structural change that differs from traditional search where ads and links occupied separate visual spaces. Ad penetration in US ChatGPT responses ranged from 51% to 72% depending on measurement source, though the data shows erratic swings rather than stable fill rates, suggesting OpenAI is still determining how much answer surface it can monetize before user friction emerges. Google is executing a parallel strategy by embedding ads into AI Mode and AI Overviews through its Performance Max and AI Max campaigns, with plans to migrate Dynamic Search Ads onto these surfaces starting in the reported month. The emergence of paid inventory directly adjacent to earned mentions undermines the foundational assumption of answer engine optimization—that securing an organic citation represents durable, unbought value—since CFOs can now compare a guaranteed Tuesday-to-Wednesday paid placement against unstable, non-purchasable organic citations that show heavy month-to-month turnover.
strategic_hook: Marketing teams need to conduct competitive audit and business case analysis comparing the ROI and defensibility of paid adjacency placements versus earned citations in AI answers, since the two now compete for attention on the same screen and only one can be guaranteed.

heading: PRACTICAL AI WORKFLOWS FOR FOUNDERS AND GTM TEAMS (2 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article outlines four practical AI workflow systems designed for founders and go-to-market teams. The Pressure Profile ICP System adds organizational pressure, role tension, behavioral triggers, and emotional context to traditional ideal customer profiles beyond basic demographics. The Context Stack organizes business information into three layers (who you are, what you're working on, how you want AI to help) to eliminate repetitive explanations in AI chats. The Content Trust Analysis System uses diagnostic prompts to evaluate content across recognition, credibility, risk reduction, and commitment dimensions to guide improvement decisions. Dynamic Workflows for GTM explains six patterns for organizing AI tasks like splitting repeated work, routing different inputs, and separating creation from critique, while the GTM Knowledge System Kit provides schemas and templates for building queryable knowledge bases from competitor research and customer insights. The author emphasizes that output verification is essential throughout, as AI can miss or invent details.
strategic_hook: Founders and GTM leaders can use the Pressure Profile ICP System to move beyond surface-level customer segmentation and build targeting strategies grounded in organizational pain points, role-specific tensions, and behavioral triggers that actually explain why buyers would adopt their solution.
